messages.subject: Problems with non-wear time and window length
messages.subject_clean: Problems with non-wear time and window length
messages.body_plain:
Hi Vincent and all,

I’m currently using GGIR to process 7-day Actigraph data. As the measurement unfortunately didn’t start at midnight, but rather during the day, the assessment period includes in fact 8 days (with half a day at the beginning and at the end of the measurement period). As we are only interested in the 6 full days in the middle, I set “timewindow” to “MM” in order to ignore the half days.

For part 2 (day summary) everything seems correct (day 1 and 8 are ignored), except for the 7th day. For each participant (n=56) I have 23.751 “N valid hours” for the 7th day.

For part 5 (day summary) a similar problem occurs. Here the second day has always a non-wear time of 0.9986 h for each participant. Additionally, for some participants the days are shifted, so that the output starts with the second day and ends with the 7th day. The window length has then also a value higher than 24 hours (e.g. 28.75 hours) for the first day.

Is there maybe a way to correct this or does somebody know why this happens? Setting ”excludefirstlast.part5” to TRUE didn’t change the problem with the non-wear time and also changing the “maxdur“-value didn’t solve the problem.

Please find the used shell script below.

Thanks in advance!

Anne Backes

library(GGIR)

             # INPUT NEEDED:

             mode=c(1,2,3,4,5),

             datadir="//myinputdir/",

             outputdir="//myoutputdir/",

             do.cal = TRUE,

             do.enmo = TRUE,

             #-------------------------------

             # Part 2

             #-------------------------------

             strategy = 2,

             maxdur = 8,

             includedaycrit = 10,

             dayborder = 0,

             winhr = 5,

             qlevels = c(0.25,0.5,0.75),

             qwindow=c(0,24),

             ilevels = c(seq(0,400,by=50),8000),

             iglevels = c(seq(0,4000,by=25),8000),

             mvpathreshold =c(100.6),

             boutduration = 120,

             #-------------------------------

             # Part 5

             #-------------------------------

             threshold.lig = c(44.8),

             threshold.vig = c(428.8),

             boutcriter.in <http://boutcriter.in> = 0.9,

             boutcriter.mvpa = 0.8,

             boutdur.in <http://boutdur.in> = c(10,20,30),

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Re: GGIR version 1.10-1 now online
messages.body_plain:
Dear Anne,
It is indeed a bug in GGIR. The conversion from numeric to character format sleep timings goes wrong.
I have now fixed this in the development version on GitHub, and will upload a new GGIR version to CRAN soon.
For the moment, you can use the numeric estimates to calculate the character estimates yourself. It is the hour relative to the previous midnight, so: 22=10pm, 24 = midnight, 30 = 6am, 36 = noon.

The reason why it caused incorrect estimates was because of my effort this summer to tidy up the code. For most parts of the code I have tests to check that I do not introduce errors, but for this part I did not have those tests yet.
Thanks again for reporting this,
Vincent

Hi Thomas,

For Part2 you set mvpathreshold. Part2 provides results with no differentiation between sleep / wake.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Charlotte,
There is no limit on the number of files GGIR can process. GGIR has been used in data sets much larger than yours.
That said, more data will demand more memory, but with only 50 files I do not expect this to be a problem.

A more likely explanation is that you ran into a file that did not wanted to process at the report generations stage. This may indicate a bug in GGIR.

If the error message would occur earlier in the process you can investigate the issue by setting: overwrite =FALSE, do.parallel=FALSE... but in your case it probably does not help.
The other thing you can do is to investigate at what specific file the analysis stops. In other words what is file 47?
Can you process it as a separate dataset?
Can you share the part 1 milestone data corresponding to file 47? (from the meta/basic/... folder).

General advise about processing large datasets:
Your approach of splitting the data is one way to do it. Another approach is to put all data in one folder with subfolders A1, A2, A3, etc and set argument storefolderstructure =TRUE. The nice thing then is that you get all your output in together in one csv overview, but there will be a column at the end indicating in which of the subfolders the file was stored.
Also you could use the f0 and f1 arguments to process specific subsets of the data.
Use overwrite=FALSE to process only the new files that have not been processed before.
I am not sure why more files would result in a slower process. Did you time the processing time and made sure that your PC is not trying to do other heavy tasks in parallel?
Best, Vincent

Dr. Vincent van Hees
Independent consultant
www.movementdata.nl <http://www.movementdata.nl>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mark,

Thanks for sharing these results. I have now been able to replicate it with my own data. Getting a full understanding of what exactly caused the change may not be easy, because a lot of code has changed since the 8th May when 1.9-1 was released. It would be rather labour intensive to figure out where exactly the critical change(s) occurred and whether they are concerning or actually desirable.

I can see in the data that tiny value differences already start to occur in the calibration coefficient, which is before function g.getmeta is applied in function g.part 1. So, possibly the search for a difference will have to start with functions g.calibrate, g.readaccfile, and the upper part of g.part1... and any function that is being used along the way. The following url shows all code changes in GGIR between the 8th of May and today: https://github.com/wadpac/GGIR/compare/0723108..75c3a76, which may help.

For many years I have approached the risk of inconsistencies as a side product of ongoing efforts to improve the open source code as a (mostly) one man team.
However, I think GGIR is now at stage that expectations become higher. I hope that the following improvements from the past 5 months will be a first step in the right direction:
- Test coverage has increased from 63% in May to 75% at the moment, which should make it easier to spot inconsistencies between versions.
- As of version 1.10-1 g.shell.GGIR stores a config.csv file with a log of all the argument values it passes on to functions g.part1, g.part2, g.part3, g.part4, and g.part5. This should make it easier to rule out a difference in input arguments when comparing GGIR versions.

Additional future efforts may go to:
- Expanding test coverage, and also the quality of the existing tests.
- Establish a clearer GGIR release process: Make habit of keeping a detailed log of whether the new version was compared to the last version and whether inconsistencies were found, if any then some degree of peer involvement to agree on the change.
- Develop commercial service to provide such guarantees, because obviously it is difficult to do all this on voluntary basis.

Regards, Vincent

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Differences between GGIR 1.9.1 to GGIR 1.10
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mark,

I have done a bit more research on this, because I am keen to understand how we can better monitor and preserve consistency.

For several years there has been a unit test in GGIR on the average value of ENMO as stored by function g.part1.
Our recent evaluation indicates that that value changed after version 1.9-1. So, either the unit test should have picked this up or I intentionally modified the unit test in response to a major change to the code.

The unit test has been stable since version 1.8-1 (January 2019)..
The code In test_chainof5parts January 4 reads expect_that(round(mean(M$metashort$ENMO),digits=5),equals(0.02894))
On January 5 in the last commit before GGIR release 1.8-1 the value changed to 0.02898
After that the value has remained the same (0.02898) across all key GGIR release dates.

I know, and the change log <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/news.html> confirms, that major improvements were made in early January to how the data is loaded. In the past there were incorrect sample shifts between days of between 1 and 100 samples depending on data format.
So, I expect this to have influence the output in January, but not to have played a role in the apparent differences between version 1.9-1 in May and the current version.

Based on the above I see two possible explanations:
1. Our comparison is not sufficiently standardised. Maybe because default argument values have changed, that we do not explicitly specify.
2. The unit test is not sensitive to the changes that may have occurred after release 1.9-1. Instead of looking at the average value, it may be important to also test for specific values.

Point 1 will hopefully be easier to check in the future with the new configfile functionality.
Point 2 is possible, but it would also mean that all unit tests are somehow insensitive to all the changes. A general review of the precision of unit tests seems desirable.

Regards,
Vincent

Getting a full understanding of what exactly caused the change may not be easy, because a lot of code has changed since the 8th May when 1.9-1 was released. It would be rather labour intensive to figure out where exactly the critical change(s) occurred and whether they are concerning or actually desirable.
>

So, possibly the search for a difference will have to start with functions g.calibrate, g.readaccfile, and the upper part of g.part1... and any function that is being used along the way. The following url shows all code changes in GGIR between the 8th of May and today: https://github.com/wadpac/GGIR/compare/0723108..75c3a76, which may help.
>
> For many years I have approached the risk of inconsistencies as a side product of ongoing efforts to improve the open source code as a (mostly) one man team.
> However, I think GGIR is now at stage that expectations become higher. I hope that the following improvements from the past 5 months will be a first step in the right direction:
> - Test coverage has increased from 63% in May to 75% at the moment, which should make it easier to spot inconsistencies between versions.
> - As of version 1.10-1 g.shell.GGIR stores a config.csv file with a log of all the argument values it passes on to functions g.part1, g.part2, g.part3, g.part4, and g.part5. This should make it easier to rule out a difference in input arguments when comparing GGIR versions.
>
> Additional future efforts may go to:
> - Expanding test coverage, and also the quality of the existing tests.
> - Establish a clearer GGIR release process: Make habit of keeping a detailed log of whether the new version was compared to the last version and whether inconsistencies were found, if any then some degree of peer involvement to agree on the change.
> - Develop commercial service to provide such guarantees, because obviously it is difficult to do all this on voluntary basis.

> Regards, Vincent

messages.body_plain:
Hi Anne,

I think the problem is that using strategy = 2 is the problem, because I originally designed that for studies who have sleeplogs and want to ignore the first and last night.
The issue you report for part 2 seems to indicate a minor bug specific the strategy=2 setting, I will add it to the Github issue tracker.

If you make the following changes to your script the output should look a lot better.
strategy = 1,
includenightcrit = 16
includedaycrit = 16,
excludefirstlast = FALSE,   #< affects part 4
excludefirstlast.part5 =TRUE, # affects part 5

When I try this the output has:
- 6 or 7 days in the part 2 output (7 days if either the first or last day has 16 hours of wear time data).
- 7 nights in the part 4 output
- 6 full days in the part 5 MM output

Best, Vincent
